conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported in these early weeks of motherhood. Today I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question survey that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling physically and emotionally over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, everything is confidential, and we can pause or stop at any time. I’ll ask each question in everyday language, and you can answer however feels most comfortable.

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has it been as much as always, a little less, or hardly at all?

I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but when my husband makes a goofy face or when the dog does something silly, I catch myself giggling. It just feels like I have to remind myself to let go and enjoy the moment, whereas before it came naturally.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I can still laugh, but it’s definitely not as automatic as it used to be. It’s like I have to push myself to find things funny, and even when I do laugh, the feeling doesn’t last long.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to little things—like my morning coffee or when my mom brings dinner—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it was before I had the baby. It’s more like “that’ll be nice” instead of “I can’t wait.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that bothered him, or I didn’t burp him right. My head knows babies just have off days, but I still catch myself wondering what I did wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit. Like, I’ll suddenly picture him spitting up in his sleep or worry that he’s too quiet in the bassinet, even though I just checked on him. I can usually talk myself down pretty quickly, but the thoughts pop up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—more like a quick jolt of “what if something’s wrong?” when he makes a weird noise or sleeps longer than I expect. It’s gone in a few seconds, and I haven’t had a full-blown scared feeling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When he won’t nap unless I’m holding him and the laundry pile keeps growing, I feel like I’m drowning a little. I usually take a breath, put him in the wrap, and chip away at one task, but it’s stressful.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it’s not that I’m too unhappy to sleep. I do lie there sometimes running through the day in my head—did I sterilize the bottles, is he gaining enough weight—but it’s more like busy-mom thoughts than sadness keeping me up.
I have felt sad or miserable

I have moments—maybe once or twice a day—where I just feel kind of heavy, like I could cry if I let myself. It usually passes when the baby smiles or when my partner checks in, but the sad feeling is definitely there, hovering.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, twice this week. Once was after a short nap when I woke up and the house was still a mess even though I’d tidied earlier—it just hit me that it never stays done. The other time was when he wouldn’t latch and I felt like my body was failing him. Both times I teared up for a few minutes, wiped my face, and kept going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’m tired and sometimes down, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again and be the mom my son needs.

You've shared that over the past week you can still laugh and look forward to small pleasures, yet it takes more effort than before and the joy feels fleeting. You described moments of <sym>unnecessary self-blame</sym> when your baby is fussy and sudden <sym>worries about his safety</sym> that pop up even when you know he is fine. On some days household tasks feel overwhelming, and once or twice a day a heavy, <sym>sad</sym> sensation lingers, leading to a couple of brief crying episodes. Despite these struggles, you have not had thoughts of harming yourself and you continue to care for your son with love and determination.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient reports reduced ability to laugh and diminished enjoyment, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a few times this week" and describes specific instances of unnecessary guilt, aligning with "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>She reports sudden, intrusive worries that arise without cause and occur 'sometimes,' fitting the 'Yes, sometimes' option.</sym>, <sym>She acknowledges frequent stress ('some days, yeah') and describes feeling overwhelmed, but shows partial coping by using strategies like baby-wearing and task-chipping, aligning with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 12 places you in the 12-13 range that indicates a high possibility of <med>postpartum depression</med> under EPDS guidelines. You endorse five items at the moderate level, reflecting <sym>loss of pleasure</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym>, and intermittent tearfulness, consistent with DSM-5 criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Because item 10 is scored 0, immediate self-harm risk is not indicated, but the cumulative mood and anxiety burden warrants prompt clinical attention to prevent worsening. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next week to discuss mood and anxiety symptoms
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or therapist trained in CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression
3. Share results with a trusted family member so they can help monitor your mood and support follow-through
4. Continue to practise small self-care steps-brief outdoor walks, accepting help with chores, five-minute breathing breaks-until professional support is in place
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track any changes after starting support or treatment
6. If you notice worsening mood, panic episodes, or any self-harm thoughts, contact your provider immediately or call a local crisis line
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient report (10-item EPDS-style inquiry):

Symptoms endorsed  
- Reduced ability to experience joy/pleasure (laughing, looking forward to events)  
- Daily low mood with tearfulness; two crying episodes this week  
- Unwarranted self-blame regarding infant care  
- Recurrent intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety  
- Episodic feeling of being overwhelmed/drowning when demands accumulate

Severity indicators  
- Mood symptoms present “once or twice daily,” transiently relieved by positive infant cues  
- No prolonged sleep disruption attributable to mood; difficulty falling asleep related to “busy-mom thoughts”  
- No panic attacks; brief startle reactions only  
- No self-harm ideation

Risk profile  
- Persistent mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms with loss of pleasure and tearfulness  
- Prominent anxiety manifested as excessive, spontaneous worries about infant well-being  
- Mild functional strain (household tasks feel unmanageable on some days)

Screening significance  
Score pattern suggests elevated risk for postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; absence of suicidal ideation. Recommend formal EPDS scoring, clinical interview, and psychoeducation; consider referral for counseling and/or medical evaluation if symptoms persist or worsen.
